# South Asia

**South Asia**, also known as the **Indian subcontinent** (or "the subcontinent"), is a triangular landmass bordered by the Himalayas in the north, the Indian Ocean in the south, and the Ganges and Indus river valleys in east and west.

*Source: [South Asia - Travel guide at Wikivoyage](https://en.wikivoyage.org/wiki/South_Asia)*

## Overview

Home to 2.08 billion people (approximately 26% of the world population), South Asia has the world's tallest mountains and is the origin of some of the world's oldest civilizations. The region is the wellspring of major world religions including Hinduism, Buddhism, Sanamahism, Sikhism, and Jainism.

## Countries

### Core South Asian Countries

| Country | Capital | Population | Key Features |
|---------|---------|------------|-------------|
| **[Bangladesh](https://en.wikivoyage.org/wiki/Bangladesh)** | Dhaka | ~170 million | Muslim-majority nation famous for its rivers, beautiful beaches, wildlife, history and culture |
| **[Bhutan](https://en.wikivoyage.org/wiki/Bhutan)** | Thimphu | ~780,000 | Buddhist-majority country influenced by Tibetan culture, tourism strictly regulated |
| **[India](https://en.wikivoyage.org/wiki/India)** | New Delhi | ~1.4 billion | Largest country with ancient cultural heritage, Himalayan Mountains, Thar Desert, diverse food and architectural masterpieces |
| **[Maldives](https://en.wikivoyage.org/wiki/Maldives)** | Malé | ~520,000 | Home to gorgeous beaches, culture influenced by India and the Middle East |
| **[Nepal](https://en.wikivoyage.org/wiki/Nepal)** | Kathmandu | ~30 million | Home to Mount Everest, birthplace of the Buddha, popular with adventure tourists, rare animals and hospitality |
| **[Pakistan](https://en.wikivoyage.org/wiki/Pakistan)** | Islamabad | ~240 million | Only country created in the name of Islam, rich in culture and history, varying climates, five of the fourteen 8,000-metre mountains |
| **[Sri Lanka](https://en.wikivoyage.org/wiki/Sri_Lanka)** | Colombo | ~22 million | Buddhist majority with significant Hindu and Muslim minorities, rich cultural heritage, stunning beaches, mountains, wildlife |

### Associated Destinations

Some destinations are sometimes considered part of South Asia, though categorized elsewhere:

- **[Afghanistan](https://en.wikivoyage.org/wiki/Afghanistan)** - Mostly part of Central Asia, but involves itself in South Asian regional organizations
- **[British Indian Ocean Territory](https://en.wikivoyage.org/wiki/British_Indian_Ocean_Territory)** - Group of islands administered by Britain, south of the Maldives (off-limits for most people)
- **[Iran](https://en.wikivoyage.org/wiki/Iran)** - Occasionally considered part of the region, but more often in the Middle East/West Asia
- **[Myanmar](https://en.wikivoyage.org/wiki/Myanmar)** (formerly Burma) - May be considered due to British India history, but usually part of Southeast Asia
- **[Tibet](https://en.wikivoyage.org/wiki/Tibet)** - Shares close cultural ties with Nepal, Bhutan, Ladakh, Sikkim and North-Eastern India

## Major Cities

| Rank | City | Country | Description |
|------|------|---------|-------------|
| 1 | **[Colombo](https://en.wikivoyage.org/wiki/Colombo)** | Sri Lanka | Largest city of Sri Lanka |
| 2 | **[Delhi](https://en.wikivoyage.org/wiki/Delhi)** | India | Culturally diverse city, home to the country's capital New Delhi |
| 3 | **[Dhaka](https://en.wikivoyage.org/wiki/Dhaka)** | Bangladesh | Thriving cultural melting pot, Bangladesh's capital |
| 4 | **[Islamabad](https://en.wikivoyage.org/wiki/Islamabad)** | Pakistan | Capital of Pakistan |
| 5 | **[Kathmandu](https://en.wikivoyage.org/wiki/Kathmandu)** | Nepal | Capital of Nepal |
| 6 | **[Karachi](https://en.wikivoyage.org/wiki/Karachi)** | Pakistan | Culturally diverse and cosmopolitan city in Pakistan's south |
| 7 | **[Malé](https://en.wikivoyage.org/wiki/Mal%C3%A9)** | Maldives | Densely packed island city, gateway to the Maldives |
| 8 | **[Mumbai](https://en.wikivoyage.org/wiki/Mumbai)** | India | Most eclectic and cosmopolitan city, famous for Bollywood |
| 9 | **[Thimphu](https://en.wikivoyage.org/wiki/Thimphu)** | Bhutan | Capital of Bhutan, surrounded by mountains |

## Other Notable Destinations

| Destination | Location | Description |
|-------------|----------|-------------|
| **[Bandarban](https://en.wikivoyage.org/wiki/Bandarban)** | Bangladesh | Hill district with trekking through unspoilt forests |
| **[Cox's Bazar](https://en.wikivoyage.org/wiki/Cox%27s_Bazar)** | Bangladesh | One of the longest sea beaches in the world |
| **[Himalayan North](https://en.wikivoyage.org/wiki/Himalayan_North)** | India | The northern Himalayan region of India |
| **[Hunza Valley](https://en.wikivoyage.org/wiki/Hunza_Valley)** | Pakistan | One of the more stunning and popular parts of Pakistan's high mountain areas |
| **[Kanyakumari](https://en.wikivoyage.org/wiki/Kanyakumari)** | India | The southernmost point of mainland India |
| **[Mohenjo-daro](https://en.wikivoyage.org/wiki/Mohenjo-daro)** | Pakistan | Spectacular archaeological site of the ancient Indus Valley Civilization |
| **[Mount Everest](https://en.wikivoyage.org/wiki/Mount_Everest)** | Nepal/China | The world's tallest mountain |
| **[Sundarbans](https://en.wikivoyage.org/wiki/Sundarbans)** | India/Bangladesh | One of the best places in South Asia to see tigers |
| **[Taj Mahal](https://en.wikivoyage.org/wiki/Taj_Mahal)** | India | The incomparable marble tomb in Agra |

## History

South Asia is the origin of four major religions: Hinduism, Buddhism, Sikhism, and Jainism. Islam was introduced by invading Arabs starting around the 7th century and rose to prominence during the Mughal Empire.

The region has a complex colonial history:

- **British Rule**: Much of South Asia was under British rule, with even nominally independent areas under British suzerainty
- **Jewel in the Crown**: India was considered the "Jewel in the Crown" of the British Empire
- **Partition**: In 1947, the region was partitioned into Hindu-majority India and Muslim-majority Pakistan, leading to massive migration and bloodshed
- **Further Divisions**: The 1971 war resulted in East Pakistan becoming Bangladesh
- **Independence**: Sri Lanka (Ceylon) became independent in 1948, Maldives in 1965

### Nepal and Bhutan
- Never formally colonized by the British
- Were under British suzerainty during the colonial era
- Nepal provided Gurkha soldiers to the British Army
- Bhutan's foreign policy was controlled by the British, then passed to India after independence

## Climate

Apart from the Himalayas, the climate is tropical with:
- **Monsoon in summer** and **dry winter**
- **Western Pakistan**: Monsoon is quite non-existent
- **Southern India**: Monsoon lasts for six months
- **Sri Lanka**: Has two monsoons - one in May, one in October/November

The region experiences diverse weather patterns due to its varied geography.

## People

South Asia is one of the world's most densely populated regions:
- **Population**: About 2.08 billion people (roughly a quarter of humanity)
- **Population Density**: 305/km² (790/sq mi) - 7 times the world average
- **Urban Features**: Very common to find narrow alleys with buildings wrapped in electric wires

## Languages

The region does not have a single lingua franca, but English is widely spoken by educated people due to British colonial influence.

### Major Languages

| Language | Spoken In | Notes |
|----------|-----------|-------|
| **English** | Throughout the region | Widely spoken by educated people, result of British colonial rule |
| **Hindi** | India, Pakistan | Also helps in Nepal (Nepali is similar) |
| **Urdu** | India, Pakistan | Mutually intelligible with Hindi |
| **Bengali** | Bangladesh, West Bengal (India) | Also understood in other eastern Indian states |
| **Punjabi** | India-Pakistan border region | Straddles the border |
| **Tamil** | Southern India, Northern Sri Lanka | Spoken across borders |

### Other Notes
- India alone is home to hundreds of languages
- Pakistan also has quite a few languages
- In major cities and tourist destinations, you can generally get by with English
- It's rare for locals to speak Western European languages other than English
- Some elderly in Pondicherry (former French India) still know French
- Some elderly in Goa (former Portuguese colony) may speak Portuguese

## Getting In

### Overland

Getting in overland to South Asia can be challenging:

- **From the West**: Relatively easy, especially from Istanbul, Turkey to New Delhi, India (also known as the Hippie Trail)
- **From Northwest**: Borders Afghanistan, which has been a war zone for several decades
- **From China**: Possible via Karakoram Highway to Nepal, but requires special permit to travel through Tibet
- **From Myanmar**: Quite a lot of bureaucracy reportedly required

### By Plane

**Major International Airports**:

#### Bangladesh
- Dhaka
- Chittagong
- Sylhet

#### Bhutan
- Paro (near Thimphu)

#### India
- Delhi
- Mumbai
- Bangalore
- Chennai
- Kolkata
- Hyderabad
- Ahmedabad
- Kochi

#### Maldives
- Male

#### Nepal
- Kathmandu

#### Pakistan
- Karachi
- Lahore
- Islamabad
- Peshawar
- Faisalabad
- Multan
- Quetta
- Sialkot

#### Sri Lanka
- Colombo

**Flight Routes**:
- West coast of North America flights arrive via Singapore and Bangkok
- East coast flights usually stopover in Europe
- Flights from Europe arrive via Dubai, Doha and other major airline hubs
- Direct flights between India and the US/UK are increasing

### By Boat

- Some cruise ships visit the region
- Possible to enter on smaller vessels
- **Warning**: Be aware of Somali pirates in the area - avoid at all costs

## Getting Around

### By Train

Rail transport varies by country:
- **India**: Most extensive rail network in South Asia (see Rail travel in India)
- **Pakistan**: Rail network mostly underdeveloped
- **Sri Lanka**: Efficient and cheap train network with beautiful hill country and tea plantation scenery
- **Bangladesh**: Famous for its overcrowded trains
- **Maldives, Nepal, Bhutan**: No trains at all

## Nature

South Asia offers dramatic natural beauty:
- **World's tallest mountains** (Himalayas, Karakoram)
- **Coastal regions** with the world's highest rainfall
- Part of the **Indomalayan wildlife region**

**Iconic Species**:
- Asian elephants
- Tigers
- Peacocks

**Notable for**:
- **Nepal** and **Kashmir**: World renowned for mountaineering

## Religion and Spirituality

South Asia is the birthplace of major religious movements:
- **Hinduism**
- **Buddhism**
- **Sikhism**
- **Jainism**

These have a long history and intercontinental appeal since the 20th century. Many visitors come to South Asia to learn **yoga** - a group of physical, mental and spiritual practices from ancient India.

## Itineraries

Popular travel routes in South Asia:

1. **[Istanbul to New Delhi overland](https://en.wikivoyage.org/wiki/Istanbul_to_New_Delhi_overland)** - The classic Hippie Trail
2. **[On the trail of Kipling's Kim](https://en.wikivoyage.org/wiki/On_the_trail_of_Kipling%27s_Kim)** - Literary journey
3. **[Grand Trunk Road](https://en.wikivoyage.org/wiki/Grand_Trunk_Road)** - Historic trade route
4. **[Karakoram Highway](https://en.wikivoyage.org/wiki/Karakoram_Highway)** - High mountain road
5. **[World Heritage Sites Tour in Sri Lanka](https://en.wikivoyage.org/wiki/World_Heritage_Sites_Tour_in_Sri_Lanka)** - Cultural heritage journey

## Sports

Popular sports in South Asia:

- **Cricket**: Huge business in South Asia, with India, Pakistan, Bangladesh and Sri Lanka boasting world-class national teams
- **Football** (soccer): Not as popular as cricket, but has a niche following, especially in Kolkata
- **Field hockey**: Popular in India and Pakistan

## See

- Sites from the empires and kingdoms making up South Asian history
- Ancient monuments and temples
- UNESCO World Heritage Sites
- Diverse cultural performances and festivals

## Buy

- **Bargaining**: Essential while shopping in most countries of the region
- **Carpets**: Both India and Pakistan have a long history of carpet manufacture
- **Arts and Crafts**: Huge range of items at attractive prices due to low labor cost

## Eat

You will not be able to experience the best of South Asian culture until you have consumed its flavorful food. India alone has some of the best cuisines in the world, with incredible diversity throughout the region.

**Notable Cuisines**:
- Indian: North and South have distinct styles
- Pakistani: Similar to North Indian
- Bangladeshi: Rich and flavorful
- Sri Lankan: Spicy and diverse
- Nepali: Influenced by Indian and Tibetan
- Bhutanese: Unique and spicy

## Drink

- **Tea** (chai): Common beverage consumed throughout the region
- **Alcohol**: Banned or restricted in Muslim communities and some Hindu-majority areas (e.g., Gujarat)
- **Fruit juices**: Ubiquitous throughout the region

## Stay Safe

**Generally Safe Areas**: Most of the region is considered safe for visitors

**Areas to Avoid**:
- **Northwest Pakistan**: Close to the border with Afghanistan, war-zone controlled by extremist militant groups such as Tehreek-e-Taliban
- **Parts of Kashmir**: Can be unsafe due to ongoing conflicts

**General Advice**:
- Avoid political demonstrations
- Be cautious in border areas
- Check travel advisories before visiting
- Respect local customs and dress codes

## Wiki Links

- [[India]] - Main India travel page
- [[Delhi]] - Capital of India
- [[Manali]] - Popular hill station in Himachal Pradesh

---

*This page is based on the Wikivoyage guide for South Asia.*

# Manali

**Manali** is a popular hill station and tourist destination in Himachal Pradesh, India. Located in the northern part of the country at the edge of the Himalayas, Manali is often called the "second home" by frequent visitors, especially those from Delhi and Chandigarh.

*Source: [Top Places To Visit In Manali](https://footloosedev.com/what-to-see-and-do-in-manali/) by Dev from Footloose Dev*

## Overview

Manali's close proximity to major North Indian cities like Delhi (approximately 12-14 hours by road) and Chandigarh (approximately 7-8 hours by road) makes it a preferred weekend getaway, especially during the summer months when the heat in Indian cities becomes unbearable.

The frequent overnight buses from Delhi to Manali make it easy to get there. Manali is not just a summer escape but also a year-round destination offering different experiences in each season.

**State**: Himachal Pradesh
**Altitude**: Approximately 2,050 meters (6,726 feet)
**Best Time to Visit**: March-April, September-November (for camping), December-February (for snow)
**Nearest Airport**: Kullu (Bhuntar), 50 km away

## Top Places to Visit in Manali

### Main Attractions

#### Manali Mall Road
- **Description**: The heart of Manali's tourist activity
- **Features**: Good food, bike rentals, adventure tours, local wear, Kashmiri Pashmina, Darjeeling Tea
- **Shopping**: Authentic Nepalese shops selling yak wool blankets and ponchos
- **Note**: Tourist trap for some, but a must-visit for first-timers
- **Tip**: Bargain hard - nothing is worth the initial price
- **Cost**: Varies by purchase

#### Manali Nature Park
- **Description**: Oasis of greenery and fresh air
- **Features**: Full of Deodar trees, houses rare Himachal state birds
- **Distance**: About half a kilometer from Mall Road
- **Entry Fee**: Small fee (check tourism website for current rates)
- **Perfect for**: Nature lovers and those seeking peace

#### Nehru Kund
- **Description**: Natural spring named after India's first Prime Minister, Jawaharlal Nehru
- **Local Belief**: Water has medicinal qualities, said to cure many diseases including cancer
- **Story**: Jawaharlal Nehru reportedly drank this water when ill and was cured
- **Features**: Hanuman Temple located right opposite the kund
- **Location**: On the way to Solang Valley

#### Rohtang Pass
- **Description**: High mountain pass at nearly 4,000 meters (13,123 feet) above sea level
- **Features**: Snow on either side, majestic views of the valley
- **Activities**: Bike trips offer incredible experiences
- **Bike Rental**: 800-2000 Rupees per day depending on the bike
- **Extended Trip**: Can be part of a Manali to Leh bike trip
- **Note**: First high pass on the Leh bike trip

#### Manu Temple
- **Description**: Dedicated to Sage Manu, believed to be the creator of the world in Hindu mythology
- **Significance**: A visit to Manali is considered incomplete without visiting Manu Temple
- **Location**: At the very end of Old Manali
- **Best Time**: During the Fagli celebrations

#### Solang Valley
- **Description**: Known for its breathtaking natural beauty
- **Activities**:
  - Paragliding
  - Zorbing
  - Skiing (during winter months)
  - Short hikes (during summer)
  - Beautiful views
- **Duration**: Can be extended to Atal Tunnel and Sissu in a day trip
- **Distance**: About 30-45 minutes from Mall Road
- **Transport**: Taxi, public buses, or drive
- **Note**: Nearly everyone who visits Manali also visits Solang Valley

#### Hadimba Temple
- **Description**: Ancient temple dedicated to Hadimba Devi, wife of the Pandava prince Bhima
- **Features**: Unique architecture amid the deodar forest
- **Significance**: Must-visit spot for its historical and architectural value
- **Distance**: 2 km from Mall Road
- **Additional**: Yak riding available (offered by many locals)

#### Vashishth Hot Spring
- **Description**: Small town known for its natural hot water springs
- **Belief**: Springs have medicinal properties
- **Features**:
  - Ancient temple dedicated to Sage Vashisht
  - Two separate bathing areas for men and women
  - Market with HEMP bags and fancy hippie pyjamas
- **Accommodation**: Less crowded lodging options available
- **Distance**: Short distance from Manali

#### Jogini Waterfall
- **Description**: Beautiful waterfall offering a pleasant hike
- **Experience**: Trek through the forest, mesmerizing view of the waterfall
- **Duration**: About 45 minutes from Vashishth
- **Video**: Available on author's YouTube channel

#### Beas River
- **Description**: The river that flows through and makes Manali popular
- **Activities**: Stroll along the banks, riverside camping
- **Accommodation**: Many riverside camping sites available
- **Perfect for**: Those wanting to experience the river up close

#### Naggar Castle
- **Description**: Historic castle with mixed reviews
- **History**: Once the residence of the King of Naggar (capital of Kullu Manali), later used by the British Raj
- **Current**: Acts as a hotel run by Himachal Tourism
- **Location**: Short distance from Manali, in the town of Naggar
- **Note**: The author didn't like it much but it's still recommended

#### Tibetan Monasteries
- **Description**: Several monasteries showcasing Tibetan art, culture, and spirituality
- **Main Monasteries**:
  - Gadhan Thekchhokling Gompa
  - Himalayan Nyingamapa Gompa
- **Offbeat Option**: Pangah Monastery on the way to Kasheri Village

#### Jana Waterfall
- **Description**: Hidden gem near Manali
- **Features**: Trek through picturesque apple orchards and forests
- **Itinerary**: Good 1-day itinerary from Manali to Naggar Castle to Jana Waterfall

## Adventure Activities in Manali

Manali is a hub for adventure sports and outdoor activities. Here are the top experiences:

### 1. Paragliding
- **Best Sites**: Solang Valley and Marhi
- **Note**: Bir (in Himachal Pradesh) is considered the best paragliding site, but Manali offers great options too

### 2. Skiing and Snowboarding
- **Best Time**: Winter months
- **Best Location**: Solang Valley
- **Organizer**: Footloose Camps (offers certified skiing and snowboarding lessons)
- **Contact**: WhatsApp 8800763430 (call only after initial WhatsApp contact)

### 3. River Rafting
- **Location**: Beas River
- **Experience**: Amazing rapids for exhilarating white-water rafting
- **Season**: May to September only
- **Note**: No rafting during heavy rains

### 4. Trekking
- **Popular Treks**:
  - Hampta Pass Trek
  - Beas Kund Trek
  - Bhrigu Lake Trek
  - Lama Dugh Trek
- **Duration**: Varies from 1-10 days
- **Note**: Manali is a hub for trekking adventures

### 5. Mountain Biking
- **Terrain**: Rugged terrain and picturesque landscapes
- **Bike Rental**: Available locally
- **Trails**: Various trails catering to different skill levels
- **Popular Routes**: Manali-Leh (10 days), Manali-Kaza (10 days)

### 6. Ziplining
- **Experience**: Thrill of zipping across valleys and gorges
- **Locations**: Solang Valley, Marhi, and other sites
- **Features**: Ziplines over the Beas River

### 7. Camping
- **Experience**: Set up camp amidst stunning natural beauty
- **Features**: Bonfires, stargazing, outdoor activities
- **Operators**: Many operators offer organized camping experiences

### 8. Rock Climbing and Rappelling
- **Activity**: Test strength and agility on rocky cliffs
- **Additional**: Rappelling down waterfalls

### 9. Hot Air Ballooning
- **Experience**: Serene yet exhilarating ride
- **Views**: Panoramic views of Manali and surroundings

### 10. Yak and Horse Riding
- **Experience**: More relaxed adventure
- **Locations**: Solang Valley and surrounding areas

### 11. Jeep Safaris
- **Experience**: Explore rugged terrain of the Himalayas
- **Features**: Remote villages, breathtaking landscapes
- **Winter**: 4×4 Gypsy rides across Solang Valley

## Safety Tips for Adventure Activities

1. **Choose Licensed Operators**: Always select licensed and reputable operators
2. **Wear Appropriate Gear**: Use proper safety equipment for each activity
3. **Follow Guidelines**: Adhere to all safety guidelines provided by experts
4. **Weather Awareness**: Be prepared for sudden changes in weather conditions, especially in mountainous regions
5. **Physical Fitness**: Ensure you're physically fit for the chosen activity

## Where to Stay in Manali

### Old Town (Recommended)
- **Distance**: 2 km from Mall Road
- **Advantages**: Better location, cheaper prices, peaceful experience
- **Features**: Easy availability of booze, scooter rentals, English Bakery
- **Accommodation**: Few dozen guest houses and hotels
- **Transport**: Walk the 2km or take auto-rickshaw for 150 Rupees
- **Off-Season**: Nice double-bed room can cost as low as 500 Rupees
- **Peak Season**: Prices shoot up during summer
- **Hostels**: Several backpacker hostels available

### Footloose Camps
- **Description**: Traditional Himachali house converted into a boutique stay
- **Location**: Hilltop with panoramic views of Manali and Kullu Valley
- **Features**: Picturesque location, unique experience

### Camping Locations

#### Riverside Camps
- **Location**: Near Beas River across Kullu Valley
- **Best Areas**: Hallan Valley
- **Features**: Offbeat places with excellent camping experiences

#### Solang Valley Area
- **Location**: On the way to Solang Valley
- **Features**: Several campsites along the route

#### Hallan Valley
- **Distance**: 25 km and 15 km from Mall Road in Manali
- **Features**: Scenic, less crowded camping spots

### Igloo Stay in Manali
- **Experience**: Experience of a lifetime
- **Description**: Stay in an igloo
- **Capacity**: Meant for 2 people
- **Availability**: About 10-15 igloos across Manali
- **Season**: Available during winter months

## Best Places to Eat in Manali

### Babushka (Vashishth)
- **Location**: In Vashishth, 2km from Manali Mall Road
- **Atmosphere**: Hippie corner with solo travelers from around the world
- **Food**: Super good food
- **Vibe**: Friendly atmosphere, great for meeting fellow travelers

### Café 1947
- **Description**: Vintage Italian café and Manali's first music café
- **Features**: Read a book, play your favorite tunes, perfect ambience
- **Suitable for**: Solo travelers and big groups alike
- **Rating**: Author's personal favorite

### Casa Bella Vista
- **Cuisine**: Spanish and Italian
- **Features**: Picturesque panoramas of surrounding mountains
- **Atmosphere**: Great views with delicious food

### Johnson's Cafe (Old Manali)
- **Location**: Very close to Mall Road, towards Old Manali
- **Cuisine**: Two locations - one offers Indian, another offers continental
- **Features**: Fine dining experience
- **Daily Event**: Live music around 6 pm every day
- **Ownership**: Belongs to siblings

### Cafe Route 24 at Footloose Camps
- **Theme**: Motorcycle/biking theme
- **Features**: Great place for hookah with a view
- **Location**: Picturesque location

## How to Reach Manali

### By Bus (Most Popular)
- **Departure Cities**: Delhi, Chandigarh
- **Frequency**: Dozens of daily buses
- **Schedule**: Most run overnight
- **Duration**:
  - From Delhi: About 12 hours (overnight journey)
  - From Chandigarh: About 7-8 hours
- **Departure Time**: Catch bus between 5pm-9pm to arrive early to late morning
- **Cost**: 1000-2000 Rupees from Delhi to Manali

### By Car (Self-Driven)
- **Navigation**: Google Maps works well
- **Route**: 4-lane highway from Delhi/Chandigarh to Manali
- **Features**: Many tunnels that save time and bypass main towns
- **Alternative**: Book a taxi (Ola Outstation available)

### By Train
- **Note**: There is no direct rail connection to Manali
- **Alternative**: Travel to nearby stations and then by road

### By Air
- **Nearest Airport**: Kullu (Bhuntar), 50 km from Manali
- **Note**: Flying is very expensive compared to road options

## Best Time to Visit Manali

### December-February (Winter)
- **Main Attraction**: Snow
- **Activities**: Skiing, snowboarding, snow activities
- **Weather**: Cold with snowfall

### March-April & September-November (Shoulder Seasons)
- **Activities**: Good time for camping
- **Advantages**: Offbeat season, fewer tourists
- **Reason**: Most people visit to escape Delhi heat

### May-June (Summer)
- **Weather**: Good in terms of weather
- **Note**: Peak tourist months, more crowded
- **Popular**: Escape from Delhi heat

### July-August (Monsoon)
- **Warning**: Not advised to visit
- **Exception**: Spiti Valley can be visited (read Spiti Valley itinerary for details)
- **Reason**: Heavy rainfall, landslides possible

## Travel Tips

1. **Best Option**: Taking a night bus from Delhi is always the best option
2. **Stay Duration**: Plan for at least 3-4 days to fully experience Manali
3. **Combined Trips**: Consider combining with nearby destinations like Leh or Spiti Valley
4. **Altitude**: Be prepared for altitude effects (2,050+ meters)
5. **Weather**: Pack for all weather conditions, even in summer

## Additional Resources

- [[India]] - Main India travel page
- [[Himachal Pradesh]] - State information
- [[Adventure Activities in India]] - More on adventure sports
- [[Best Time to Visit India]] - Seasonal guide

---

# Delhi

**Delhi** is the capital city of India and one of the oldest continuously inhabited cities in the world. With a history spanning over 5,000 years, Delhi offers an overwhelming amount of history, culture, life, food, temples, and everything else you could possibly imagine.

*Source: [25 Incredible Things To Do In Delhi, India](https://migrationology.com/25-things-to-do-in-delhi-india/) by Mark Wiens*

## Overview

Delhi is a giant metropolis that serves as the political, cultural, and commercial center of India. The city is a fascinating blend of ancient history and modern development, with Mughal-era monuments standing alongside contemporary buildings. While visiting Delhi can present challenges - things don't always turn out as planned and frustrations can arise - the culture, history, and food make it an incredible destination.

**Population**: ~30 million (National Capital Region)
**Best Time to Visit**: October to March (cooler temperatures)
**Language**: Hindi, English widely spoken

## Where to Stay

Delhi offers accommodations for every budget:

### High End
- **Oberoi New Delhi** - One of the best luxury hotels in the city

### Mid-range
- **Saket Bed and Breakfast** - Feels like staying in a luxury home, extremely well furnished, clean, safe, in a nice South Delhi neighborhood
- **Bloomrooms** - Flash-packer style mid-range place in South Delhi

### Budget
- **Smyle Inn** - Located in Paharganj area near the railroad station, good budget option

See also: [[Where to stay in Delhi]]

## Transportation

### Metro
The Delhi Metro is clean, efficient, often packed, and extremely cheap. To make travel easier:
- Buy a Metro card (50 Rupees deposit) and add cash
- 1-day tourist passes: 100 Rupees
- 3-day tourist passes: 250 Rupees

After getting off the Metro, you can either walk or take a short auto rickshaw ride to most attractions.

### HOHO Bus (Hop On Hop Off)
- Tourist bus with 1-day or 2-day passes
- Goes from attraction to attraction
- Buses come every 30-45 minutes
- **Note**: Does not run on Mondays

### Auto Rickshaws
- Always negotiate the price before getting in
- Short rides typically cost 30-50 INR

## Top 25 Things to Do in Delhi

### Temples & Religious Sites

#### 1. The Lotus Temple (Bahá'í House of Worship)
- **Description**: Designed in the shape of a sacred lotus flower with 27 marble petals
- **Religion**: Open to all religions (Bahá'í philosophy)
- **Features**: Nicely manicured gardens, free shoe deposit, silent sanctuary
- **How to get there**: Metro to Kalkaji Mandir station, 10-minute walk
- **Website**: [bahaihouseofworship.in](http://www.bahaihouseofworship.in/)
- **Hours**: Tuesday-Sunday 9am-7pm, closed Mondays
- **Price**: Free

#### 2. ISKCON Hare Krishna Temple
- **Description**: One of the largest temples dedicated to the International Society for Krishna Consciousness
- **Features**: Free to walk around, sit in sanctuary, listen to drum and chant of "Har-e-Krishna"
- **How to get there**: Closest Metro station is Nehru Place, 10-minute walk
- **Website**: [iskcondelhi.com](http://www.iskcondelhi.com/)
- **Address**: Hare Krishna Hill Sant Nagar, East of Kailash New Delhi
- **Hours**: Day hours
- **Price**: Free

#### 3. Kalkaji Mandir Hindu Temple
- **Description**: Dedicated to the Goddess Kali, mostly visited by locals
- **Features**: Site of many rituals including singing and chanting
- **How to get there**: Metro to Kalkaji Mandir station, 5-minute walk (across from Lotus Temple entrance)
- **Hours**: Tuesday-Sunday morning to night, closed Mondays
- **Price**: Free

#### 4. Jama Masjid
- **Description**: Largest Islamic mosque in Delhi, built in the 17th century
- **Features**: Huge structure with towering minarets and onion-shaped domes, capacity for 25,000 people
- **Note**: Camera fee is 300 INR, but entrance is free if not taking photos
- **How to get there**: Metro to Chawri Chowk, exit Gate #3, walk 10-15 minutes
- **Hours**: 8am-30 minutes before sunset
- **Price**: Free to enter, 300 INR for photos

#### 5. Akshardham Temple
- **Description**: Modern Hindu temple complex built in 2005 with elaborate architecture
- **Features**: Secure free storage for belongings, stunning interior with unimaginable detail
- **Note**: No photos allowed inside
- **How to get there**: Metro to Akshardham station, 10-minute walk
- **Website**: [akshardham.com](http://www.akshardham.com/)
- **Hours**: 9:30am-6:30pm, closed Monday
- **Price**: Free

#### 6. Gurudwara Bangla Sahib (Sikh Temple)
- **Description**: One of the most significant Sikh temples in Delhi
- **Features**: Friendly, inviting atmosphere, huge pool of water, dining facility, medical facility
- **How to get there**: Metro to Patel Chowk, 10-15 minute walk along Ashok Road
- **Hours**: Daytime hours
- **Price**: Free

#### 7. Laxmi Narayan Mandir (Birla Mandir)
- **Description**: Significant Hindu temple complex, officially opened by Mahatma Gandhi
- **Features**: Hindu temple for people of all castes
- **Note**: Shoe storage expects a tip
- **How to get there**: Auto rickshaw from Sikh Temple for 40 INR
- **Hours**: 6am-10pm daily
- **Price**: Free (tip for shoes expected)

### Historical Sites

#### 8. Hauz Khas Complex
- **Description**: Ancient community of ruins including a mosque, various tombs, and a historic water tank
- **History**: Built in early 1300s to store rainwater
- **Features**: Now a public park, popular with students
- **How to get there**: Metro to Green Park, then auto rickshaw (20-30 INR)
- **Website**: [hauzkhasvillage.in](http://hauzkhasvillage.in/)
- **Hours**: Daylight hours
- **Price**: Free

#### 9. Lodi Gardens
- **Description**: Public park scattered with ancient Mughal tombs and structures
- **Features**: Kids play, picnics, artists find inspiration, large park for walking
- **How to get there**: Metro to Khan Market, 30-minute walk or auto rickshaw
- **Hours**: Daylight hours
- **Price**: Free

#### 10. India Gate
- **Description**: 42-meter tall war memorial built in 1931
- **Features**: Honors Indian soldiers, continual flame under the gate
- **Warning**: Many beggars and pushy sellers in the area
- **How to get there**: Nearest Metro is Central Secretariat, 30-minute walk along Rajpath
- **Hours**: Daylight hours
- **Price**: Free

#### 11. Jantar Mantar
- **Description**: Complex of structures used for astronomy observations
- **History**: Commissioned by Mughal emperor Muhammad Shah, constructed by Maharaja Jai Singh II
- **Features**: 13 different instruments for sun, moon, and planet measurements
- **How to get there**: Metro to Rajiv Chowk or Patel Chowk, short walk along Sansad Marg
- **Address**: Sansad Marg, Connaught Place, New Delhi
- **Website**: [jantarmantar.org](http://www.jantarmantar.org/)
- **Hours**: Daylight hours
- **Price**: 100 INR

#### 12. Qutub Minar
- **Description**: 72.5-meter minaret, tallest in India, built nearly 1,000 years ago
- **Features**: Constructed from red sandstone with detailed carvings, UNESCO World Heritage Site
- **Note**: Cannot go inside, but impressive from distance and up close
- **How to get there**: Metro to Qutub Minar station, then auto rickshaw (30-40 INR)
- **Address**: Mehrauli, New Delhi, Delhi 110030
- **Hours**: 10am-6pm daily
- **Price**: 250 INR (count your change!)

#### 13. Humayun's Tomb
- **Description**: Persian-designed tomb built in mid-1500s for Mughal emperor Humayun
- **Features**: Surrounded by gardens, climb stairs to main deck, see marble tombstones inside
- **How to get there**: No direct Metro, closest is Khan Market or JLN Stadium, then auto rickshaw
- **Address**: Mathura Road, Nizamuddin, New Delhi
- **Hours**: 6am-6pm daily
- **Price**: 250 INR (UNESCO World Heritage Site)

#### 14. Tomb of Safdarjung
- **Description**: Built in 1754 for Safdarjung, a prominent leader under Muhammad Shah
- **Features**: Similar construction to Humayun's tomb, surrounded by Mughal gardens
- **How to get there**: Metro to Safdarjung station, exit Gate 2, u-turn, few hundred meters walk
- **Hours**: Daylight hours
- **Price**: 100 INR

#### 15. Red Fort (Lal Qila)
- **Description**: Red sandstone Mughal fortress with walls surrounding an ancient city
- **Features**: Walk around, view main structures, halls, mosques, quiet escape from crowds
- **How to get there**: Walk 20 minutes or auto rickshaw from Chandni Chowk Metro to Lahore Gate
- **Address**: Netaji Subhash Rd, Chandni Chowk, New Delhi, Delhi 110006
- **Hours**: Tuesday-Sunday daylight hours, closed Mondays
- **Price**: 250 INR

### Museums & Cultural Sites

#### 16. National Museum of New Delhi
- **Description**: Impressive collection of over 200,000 individual pieces of art
- **Note**: The author didn't visit, but recommends for art and history lovers
- **How to get there**: Metro to Central Secretariat, walk towards Rajpath to Janpath
- **Address**: Janpath Road, Rajghat, New Delhi 110002
- **Website**: [nationalmuseumindia.gov.in](http://www.nationalmuseumindia.gov.in/)
- **Hours**: 10am-5pm Tuesday-Sunday, closed Monday
- **Price**: 300 INR (includes audio tour)

#### 17. Raj Ghat - Gandhi Memorial
- **Description**: Memorial dedicated to Mahatma Gandhi at the place where he was cremated
- **Features**: Park area, leave shoes at counter for small tip, walk around black marble memorial
- **How to get there**: Auto rickshaw from Chandni Chowk (60 INR), or to Indraprasta leaving (40 INR)
- **Hours**: 5:30am-7pm daily
- **Price**: Free (20 INR tip for shoe man)

### Markets & Shopping

#### 18. Chandni Chowk & Chawri Bazar
- **Description**: Dense chaotic center of trade, business, food, spices, and life
- **Features**: Narrow ancient lanes, interesting people and businesses, visit Jama Masjid and Red Fort nearby
- **Tip**: Don't miss Paranthe Wali Gali or chaat from Natraj
- **How to get there**: Metro to Chawri Bazar or Chandni Chowk station
- **Hours**: Day and night, recommended late morning to afternoon

#### 19. Spice Market (Khari Baoli in Old Delhi)
- **Description**: Largest spice market in Asia
- **Features**: Colorful array of spices, dried fruits, nuts, rickshaw transporters
- **How to get there**: Metro to Chandni Chowk, walk west along Chandni Chowk road to T-intersection, right on Mission Church Road, left on Khari Baoli

#### 20. Dilli Haat - Handicraft Village
- **Description**: Outdoor shopping plaza with high-quality Indian handicrafts
- **Features**: Safe, organized, convenient environment, represents each state of India
- **Food**: Sample Indian food from around the entire nation
- **How to get there**: Metro to INA station, short walk
- **Address**: Sri Aurobindo Marg, West Kidwai Nagar, New Delhi
- **Website**: [dillihaat.net.in](http://www.dillihaat.net.in/)
- **Hours**: 10:30am-10pm daily
- **Price**: 20 INR entrance fee

### Modern Areas

#### 21. Connaught Place - Rajiv Chowk (& Palika Bazar)
- **Description**: Central business district with series of roundabouts
- **Features**: Countless stores, delicious restaurants, dark underground shopping plaza (Palika Bazar)
- **Note**: Can be confusing for first-time visitors
- **How to get there**: Metro to Rajiv Chowk station, any exit
- **Hours**: Shops and restaurants start opening at 10-11am daily

#### 22. Paharganj (Main Bazar)
- **Description**: District next to New Delhi Railroad Station, budget backpacker center
- **Features**: Crowded streets, shopping, many businesses and restaurants
- **Food Tip**: Best chole bhature at Sita Ram Diwan Chand
- **How to get there**: Metro to New Delhi Station, walk through railroad station to other side, cross street
- **Road**: Main Bazar or Baba Namdev Marg

### Food Experiences

#### 23. Kulle Chaat
- **Description**: Various vegetables and fruits hollowed out and filled with blend of spices, lime juice, salt, chickpeas, and pomegranate seeds
- **Note**: Simple but life-changingly delicious
- **Warning**: May contain unclean water, be careful if you have a sensitive stomach
- **How to get there**: Metro to Chawri Chowk, Gate 3, walk straight down hectic road on left side
- **Price**: 50 INR

#### 24. Delhi Street Food
- **Description**: Marvelous array of Indian street food
- **Popular Items**: Chole (spicy chickpea curry), samosas, pakoras, various chaats
- **Best Location**: Chandni Chowk for diverse selection
- **Prices**: 30-50 INR for snacks, 40-60 INR for meals
- **Note**: Delhi street food is slightly more expensive than Kolkata

#### 25. North Indian Food
- **Description**: Rich, flavorful, and very satisfying cuisine
- **Features**: Breads like tandoori roti, chapatis, naan, fried breads more common than rice
- **Dishes**: Tandoori cooked chicken, paneer cheese in various curries, legumes like lentils, beans, and peas
- **Recommendations**: Karim's in Old Delhi, Bhape Da Hotel at Connaught Place
- **Note**: Both pure vegetarian and non-vegetarian restaurants available

## Practical Tips

1. **Count Your Change**: Officials may try to shortchange tourists. Always count your money.
2. **Dress Modestly**: Especially for women, avoid fancy or revealing clothing. Consider a head covering/scarf.
3. **Stay Positive**: Things won't always go as planned, but keep a positive attitude.
4. **Bargain**: Haggling is expected and can be fun. Typically pay about 1/3 of the starting price.
5. **Safety**: Generally safe, but be cautious of pickpockets in crowded areas.

## Additional Resources

- [[Delhi Travel Guide]] - Comprehensive guide with more tips
- [[Where to stay in Delhi]] - Detailed accommodation information
- [[India]] - Main India travel page
- [[South Asia Overview]] - Regional context

---

*This page is based on the guide "25 Incredible Things To Do In Delhi, India" by Mark Wiens, published April 9, 2013.*

## India Travel Guide

[Photo © Ardy](https://guide.travellerspoint.com/photos/stream/photoID/278935/features/countries/India/)

## Introduction

[![Intermit](https://photos.travellerspoint.com/274590/thumb_Bhaskar-Intermit.jpg)](https://www.travellerspoint.com/photos/stream/photoID/785120/features/countries/India/)

#### Intermit

© [geniusgene](https://www.travellerspoint.com/users/geniusgene/)

**India** 's civilization stretches back at least 5,000 years and, remarkably, has been maintained to an extremely high level in the 20th century. Whereas other [Asian](https://www.travellerspoint.com/guide/Asia/) nations have seen the decline of traditional culture, Indians, particularly those away from the major cities, maintain their traditional way of life. Thus, traveling to India is very much an unforgettable experience, as it is in many ways confronting to western notions. It is confronting when you set foot in [Delhi](https://www.travellerspoint.com/guide/Delhi/), where pollution is likely to revolt you with its stench. And it is confronting when you notice Hindu's entrenched class system and ill-treated outcasts. But while India may send your Western ideas of humanity into torrents of outrage, it will also doubtlessly impress you with some of the less confronting aspects of Indian cultural heritage: the glorious [Taj Mahal](https://www.travellerspoint.com/guide/Taj_Mahal/) in [Agra](https://www.travellerspoint.com/guide/Agra/) and dozens of other beautiful temples, the traditionally beautiful state of [Kerala](https://www.travellerspoint.com/guide/Kerala/) (often referred to as God's Own Country), rich cultural and architectural heritage in [Rajasthan](https://www.travellerspoint.com/guide/Rajasthan/) & [Tamil Nadu](https://www.travellerspoint.com/guide/Tamil_Nadu/), Indians' love for cricket and a cuisine that is simply superb.

With a population of over one billion, no single country is so multi-faceted and laden with contradictions. Culturally India might very well be the most diverse place in the world. India’s immensely varied art, history, religions, and traditions are organically woven together into an intricate tapestry. Its infinite variety favours you with different facets of fascination every time you visit. To travel in India is to expand one’s notion of the possible configurations of human society. Journeys to India can be complex and challenging, but they are always supremely rewarding.

There are so many aspects to India's personality and it is definitely a place of extremes and strange contrasts. For this reason it can be an overwhelming place, but never dull or predictable. You never know what fascinating sight may confront or astound you around the next corner. It can be quite mind boggling at times so you definitely need to do your research before you go and keep an open mind, plus take a good travel guidebook with you for reference along the way. Your attitude, dress code and behaviour will always have some bearing on how you are treated. As a tourist haggling for a good price is quite good fun and part of being in India. It won't take long before you have a good feel for what things should cost - often about a third of the starting price!! If both parties are happy with the price then the haggling should stop. It is an embarrassment to all concerned if relatively wealthy tourists end up haggling bitterly over just a few rupees. It should usually be a friendly exchange involving a bit of banter and reasoning rather than a fight.

If you wear tight or revealing clothing and are female, this will invite a lot more hassle and attention from local men. However, if you cover up and dress un-provocatively you may still not be able to avoid the stares and questioning 'eve-teasing' as it is referred to locally. Indian men seem to have quite fixed ideas about western women and in comparison to traditional Indian women men have much more freedom, are not chaperoned and so are more 'available' to Indian eyes. This kind of hassle can be annoying, but rarely threatening to women travelling alone.

## Brief History

The history of India begins with human settlement that has been confirmed to over 9,000 years ago in the central Indian state of [Madhya Pradesh](https://www.travellerspoint.com/guide/Madhya_Pradesh/). However, evidence of human activity shows the presence of Homo sapiens as long as 75,000 years ago and hominids from about 500,000 years ago. The Indus Valley Civilization, which spread and flourished in the north-western part of the Indian subcontinent from 3300 to 1300 BC, was the first major civilization in India.

The whole subcontinent was conquered by the **Maurya Empire** during the 4th and 3rd centuries BC. It subsequently became fragmented, with various parts ruled by numerous Middle kingdoms for the next 1,500 years. This is known as the classical period of India, during which India is estimated to have had the largest economy of the ancient and medieval world controlling between one third and one fourth of the world's wealth up to the 18th century.

The southern state of Kerala had maritime business links with the Roman Empire from around 77 AD. Islam was introduced in Kerala through this route by Muslim traders. Muslim rule in the subcontinent began in 712 AD when the Arab general Muhammad bin Qasim conquered Sindh and Multan in southern Punjab, setting the stage for several successive invasions between the 10th and 15th centuries AD from Central Asia, leading to the formation of Muslim empires in the Indian subcontinent such as the Delhi Sultanate and the Mughal Empire.

Mughal rule came to cover most of the northern parts of the subcontinent. Mughal rulers introduced middle-eastern art and architecture to India. The Mughal Empire suffered a gradual decline in the early eighteenth century, which provided opportunities for the Afghans, Balochis and Sikhs to exercise control over large areas in the northwest of the subcontinent until the British East India Company gained ascendancy over South Asia.

Beginning in the mid-18th century and over the next century, India was gradually annexed by the British East India Company. Dissatisfaction with Company rule led to the First War of Indian Independence, after which India was directly administered by the British Crown and witnessed a period of both rapid development of infrastructure and economic decline. During the first half of the 20th century, a nationwide struggle for independence was launched by the Indian National Congress, and later joined by the Muslim League. The subcontinent gained independence from the [United Kingdom](https://www.travellerspoint.com/guide/United_Kingdom/) in 1947, after being partitioned into the dominions of India and Pakistan.

## Geography

India is a vast country and that is why this region (which also includes [Pakistan](https://www.travellerspoint.com/guide/Pakistan/), [Sri Lanka](https://www.travellerspoint.com/guide/Sri_Lanka/) and [Nepal](https://www.travellerspoint.com/guide/Nepal/)) is popularly known as the "Indian Sub-continent". The term gives an idea about the vastness and diversity found in this region. India borders Pakistan at the Punjab Plain and the Thar desert in the west, [China](https://www.travellerspoint.com/guide/China/), [Tibet](https://www.travellerspoint.com/guide/Tibetan_Autonomous_Region/), [Nepal](https://www.travellerspoint.com/guide/Nepal/) and [Bhutan](https://www.travellerspoint.com/guide/Bhutan/) in the north in the Himalayas and [Bangladesh](https://www.travellerspoint.com/guide/Bangladesh/), along the watershed region of the Indo-Gangetic Plain, the Khasi hills and Mizo Hillsand, and [Myanmar](https://www.travellerspoint.com/guide/Myanmar/), along the Chin Hills and Kachin Hills, in the east. India is bounded to the southwest by the Arabian Sea, to the southeast by the Bay of Bengal and the [Indian Ocean](https://www.travellerspoint.com/guide/Indian_Ocean/) to the south. The southernmost part of India however is Indira Point in the [Andaman and Nicobar Islands](https://www.travellerspoint.com/guide/Andaman_and_Nicobar_Islands/). South of India are both [Sri Lanka](https://www.travellerspoint.com/guide/Sri_Lanka/) and the [Maldives](https://www.travellerspoint.com/guide/Maldives/). The Lakshadweep islands to the west are another main island group.

India hosts a major portion of the highest mountain ranges in the world, the [Himalayas](https://www.travellerspoint.com/guide/Himalayas/) (Kanchenjunga in Sikkim at 8,598 metres is the highest point), located in the northern end of the country. Going south, the land gradually descends into low lying areas with few mountains, but some hilly areas.

The Ganges is the longest river in India and forms the Indo-Gangetic Plain. The Ganges-Brahmaputra system occupies most of northern, central and eastern India. The Central Highlands is divided into three main plateaus - the Malwa Plateau in the west, the Deccan Plateau in the south (covering much of the Indian peninsula) and the Chota Nagpur Plateau in the east. The Malwa Plateau is spread across [Rajasthan](https://www.travellerspoint.com/guide/Rajasthan/), Madhya Pradesh and [Gujarat](https://www.travellerspoint.com/guide/Gujarat/). The Chota Nagpur Plateau is situated in eastern India, covering much of Jharkhand and adjacent parts of [Orissa](https://www.travellerspoint.com/guide/Orissa/), Bihar and Chhattisgarh. The Deccan Plateau occupies most of southern India.

On the southern end, India has a coastline which measures over 7,600 kilometres, from Gujarat in the west via Mumbai, Goa and [Kerala](https://www.travellerspoint.com/guide/Kerala/) to the south and up north again to [Chennai](https://www.travellerspoint.com/guide/Chennai/), Orissa and [Kolkata](https://www.travellerspoint.com/guide/Kolkata/). Especially in the southern portions, like Cochi and [Goa](https://www.travellerspoint.com/guide/Goa/), there are great beaches.

## Sights and Activities

### Taj Mahal

India's most famous attraction, the [Taj Mahal](https://www.travellerspoint.com/guide/Taj_Mahal/), is a mausoleum in [Agra](https://www.travellerspoint.com/guide/Agra/) that was constructed under Mughal Emperor Shah Jahan in memory of his favorite wife, Mumtaz Mahal who died after giving birth to their son.

### Agra Fort

The imposing Agra Fort at [Agra](https://www.travellerspoint.com/guide/Agra/) is something which should not be missed. The construction of this fort was started by Mughal Emperor Akbar and later on additional building were added by his son and grandson. The fort complex has numerous building of importance like the Moti Masjid, Sheesh Mahal, Jehangir’s Palace, Deewane-E-Am and Deewane-E-Khas.

### Kerala

The state of [Kerala](https://www.travellerspoint.com/guide/Kerala/), divided into 14 districts has emerged as one of the hottest tourist destination in India over the period of years. This place is also famous for its Backwaters. Kerala’s culture cannot be confined to a specific race or a custom, its composite in nature with its religious traditions, festivals, performing arts (dances, ballets, opera) music, martial arts, paintings, arts and crafts, The cultural heritage of Kerala is also revealed in its varied costumes and cuisine.

### Khajuraho

[Khajuraho](https://www.travellerspoint.com/guide/Khajuraho/) is a town located in Madhya Pradesh famous for groups of Hindu and Jain temples. These temples are a [UNESCO World Heritage Site](https://www.travellerspoint.com/guide/UNESCO_World_Heritage_List/) for their beautiful and erotic rock carvings. About 20 temples remain today, dating back to the 10th and 11th century A.D.

### Dharamsala/McLeod Ganj

[Dharamsala](https://www.travellerspoint.com/guide/Dharamsala/) /McLeod Ganj is located in the Kangra district of [Himachal Pradesh](https://www.travellerspoint.com/guide/Himachal_Pradesh/). Situated on the Dhauladhar Range, whose highest peak, "Hanuman Ka Tibba", at about 5,639 metres, lies just behind it, it is known as "Little Lhasa" or "Dhasa" (a short form of Dharamsala used mainly by Tibetans) because of its large population of Tibetan refugees. The Tibetan government-in-exile is headquartered in McLeodGanj.

### Shimla

[Shimla](https://www.travellerspoint.com/guide/Shimla/) is the capital city of Himachal Pradesh. In 1864, Shimla was declared the summer capital of the British Raj in India. A popular tourist destination, Shimla is often referred to as the queen of hills. Located in the northwest [Himalayas](https://www.travellerspoint.com/guide/Himalayas/) at an average altitude of 2,205 metres, the city of Shimla, draped in forests of pine, rhododendron, and oak, experiences pleasant summers and cold, snowy winters. The city is famous for its buildings styled in 'Tudorbethan' and neo-Gothic architecture dating from the colonial era.

### Wildlife watching

India is one of the best countries outside [Africa](https://www.travellerspoint.com/guide/Africa/) and probably the best in [Asia](https://www.travellerspoint.com/guide/Asia/) to watch wildlife. Wildlife include the Asian Big Five (leopard, lion, elephant, rhino and asian buffalo) but there is one animal that even is more impressive and elusive. That animal is the tiger and seeing one is a matter of luck and staying long enough in several national parks that offer this opportunity. [Kanha National Park](https://www.travellerspoint.com/guide/Kanha_National_Park/) and [Bandhavgarh National Park](https://www.travellerspoint.com/guide/Bandhavgarh_National_Park/) in [Madhya Pradesh](https://www.travellerspoint.com/guide/Madhya_Pradesh/) are among the best in the country with the highest density and chance to see this massive cat. Also, Pench and Panna Reserves are well worth a visit, though numbers of tigers have been decreasing enormously here during the last years. It is believed that Panna even lost of all its tigers due to poaching, just like Sariska reserve before. Although Ranthambore is equally famous, tiger population here has dropped recently due to poachers still active in the area. Also the [Corbett National Park](https://www.travellerspoint.com/guide/Corbett_National_Park/), around 240 kilometres north of Delhi, at the foothills of the [Himalayas](https://www.travellerspoint.com/guide/Himalayas/), is a good place to see a tiger, though you have to spend some time here and be lucky.

Many other wildlife can be spotted as well in many of the parks, including wild boar, sloth bear, rhino, elephant, gaur, Indian Gazelle, wild dogs and striped hyena. In the mountains, the very elusive snow leopard lives at altitudes of 2,000 metres upwards.

Four other parks to be visited which, because of its outstanding natural beauty and significance, are on the [Unesco World Heritage list](https://www.travellerspoint.com/guide/Unesco_World_Heritage_list/) as well. These are [Kaziranga National Park](https://www.travellerspoint.com/guide/Kaziranga_National_Park/) and [Manas National Park](https://www.travellerspoint.com/guide/Manas_National_Park/) in the northeastern state of [Assam](https://www.travellerspoint.com/guide/Assam/), the [Sundarbans National Park](https://www.travellerspoint.com/guide/Sundarbans_National_Park/), which India shares with [Bangladesh](https://www.travellerspoint.com/guide/Bangladesh/) and the [Keoladeo National Park](https://www.travellerspoint.com/guide/Keoladeo_National_Park/) in the Bharatpur district of [Rajasthan](https://www.travellerspoint.com/guide/Rajasthan/), which is particulary interesting because of its birdlife, including the rare Siberian crane.

Sasan Gir National Reserve in [Gujarat](https://www.travellerspoint.com/guide/Gujarat/) is the only place in [Asia](https://www.travellerspoint.com/guide/Asia/) which has Asian lions. Plans to relocate some lions to other reserves have not been succesful, because of resistance of local people.

### The Sundarbans

The [Sundarbans](https://www.travellerspoint.com/guide/Sundarbans/) mangrove forest is one of the largest forests of its kind and is located in the west of India and the southwest of Bangladesh on the delta of the Ganges, Brahmaputra and Meghna rivers on the Bay of Bengal. The Sundarbans are shared with [Bangladesh](https://www.travellerspoint.com/guide/Bangladesh/) and form a [UNESCO World Heritage Site](https://www.travellerspoint.com/guide/UNESCO_World_Heritage_List/). It contains a complex network of tidal waterways, mudflats and small islands of salt-tolerant mangrove forests and has a high biodiversity with a wide range of flora and fauna. Animals include 260 bird species, the Royal Bengal tiger and other threatened species such as the estuarine crocodile and the Indian python. Some of the wildlife though is very elusive and it is a matter of luck for example to see a tiger. It is best to arrange tours from Dhaka or Kulna which can last for a week if you want.

### Rajasthan

[Rajasthan](https://www.travellerspoint.com/guide/Rajasthan/) is one of the most visited parts of India and it has several great cities to visit, including [Jaisalmer](https://www.travellerspoint.com/guide/Jaisalmer/), [Jaipur](https://www.travellerspoint.com/guide/Jaipur/), [Udaipur](https://www.travellerspoint.com/guide/Udaipur/) and [Jodhpur](https://www.travellerspoint.com/guide/Jodhpur/). All these cities have their own characteristics, fortresse, maharadja palace and even colours (pink city, blue city). A trip by camel in the Thar desert also is a fantastic experience.

### Varanasi

According to Hindu mythology, [Varanasi](https://www.travellerspoint.com/guide/Varanasi/) is considered to be one of the holiest cities in India. It lies along the banks of the sacred Ganges River, and it's believed that taking a dip in it washes away all the sins and purify the soul.

The Thar desert is arid region in the northwest of the Indian subcontinent. It covers much of [Rajasthan](https://www.travellerspoint.com/guide/Rajasthan/), extending from here into the southern [Haryana](https://www.travellerspoint.com/guide/Haryana/) and [Punjab](https://www.travellerspoint.com/guide/Punjab/) states and into northern [Gujarat](https://www.travellerspoint.com/guide/Gujarat/) state. It is a hilly desert, with large areas of sand dunes, although the central part is more of a plain with no dunes at all. Unlike much of India, it hasn't got a monsoon season as wet as other parts of the country, although also here the wetter months are from July to October. It's also a good region to see lots of animals typical for this part of India and there are some interesting cities within its boundaries as well, including [Jodhpur](https://www.travellerspoint.com/guide/Jodhpur/) and the 'capital' of the desert [Jaisalmer](https://www.travellerspoint.com/guide/Jaisalmer/), where camel rides into the desert are one of the more popular trips.

If you are willing to adjust a little bit, you will be able to make the most of the local festivities and religious observances you are most likely to encounter. Even if you are mainly visiting one of the big cities, make it a point to see the surrounding rural areas. You will be stunned by the many natural marvels and genuine peasants and herders you are going to meet there. Do not feel intimidated by their traditions. Indians tend to be very curious by nature. Your visit to the most far-off places will generally not be perceived as an intrusion - quite the contrary: people will seize the opportunity and pour all their curiosity on you.

## Events and Festivals

- [Pushkarfestival](http://www.pushkarfestival.com/ "This is an external link") - one of the biggest camel fairs in the world, held in Pushkar, Rajasthan. Thousands of people during this day go to the banks of the Pushkar Lake where the fair takes place and where livestock livestock, including camels, cows, sheep and goats, is sold. A camel race marks the start off the festival, and music, songs and exhibitions are held throughout the day. Although the dates of Pushkar Fair depend upon the movement of the moon, traditionally it mostly falls in November. It falls on the day of Poornima (full moon night) in the month of Karthika. On this day, according to legend, the Hindu god Brahma sprung up the lake, so thousands of Hindu devotees take dip in the Pushkar lake, washing away the sins. The water of the lake is believed to have healing properties.
- **Holi** is quite popular in the Indian sub-continent and is traditionally celebrated on the day after the full moon in the month of Phalguna (early March), according to Hindu callendar. Holi is a thanksgiving festival, where people offer prayer to God for good harvest and fertility of the land. However it has a legend attached to it according to which an arrogant king resents his son Prahlada from worshipping Lord Vishnu. He attempts to kill his son but fails each time, finally he asks his sister Holika, who is said to be immune to burning, sits with Prahlada in fire. However Prahlada emerges alive and Holika is burnt to death. Holi commemorates this event from the Hindu mythology, and huge bonfires are burnt on the eve of Holi as its symbolic representation. This festival is also associated with the immortal love story of Krishna and Radha, and hence celebrations are spread over a period of 2 weeks in Vrindavan and Mathura - the two cities associated with Krishna. Holi is a festival of freedom from social norms and caste inhibitions are shed for a day as people indulge in fun and merry-making. Colors and 'gulal' are showered on the people dressed up for the occasion and the whole community seems to merge into one big family under the guise of colors, without any distinction whatsoever. Children with face smeared with colors run around with 'pichkaris' (big syringes to splash colored water) and play amongst themselves. People exchange good wishes, sweets and gifts. Holi is also marked by vibrant processions which are accompanied by folk songs, dances and drum beating. Parties are also organized where snacks and the traditional milk-based drink “Thandai” is served which is often intoxicated with “Bhang”. Of late, lots of foreigners have started taking interest in this festival and they even enjoy the colors and the intoxicating drink. It is advised to cover your hair with a cap and eyes with sunglasses to avoid the colors splashing the eyes and damaging the hair.
- **Thaipsum** is an important festival celebrated mainly by the Tamil community in the southern states of [India](https://www.travellerspoint.com/guide/India/) and in parts of [Malaysia](https://www.travellerspoint.com/guide/Malaysia/), [Singapore](https://www.travellerspoint.com/guide/Singapore/) and [Sri Lanka](https://www.travellerspoint.com/guide/Sri_Lanka/). The festival actually celebrates the birthday of the Hindu God Subramaniam. It is time for prayers and devotees seek divine intervention for fulfillment of their wishes. Devotees walk long distances carrying offering to reach the temple of the Lord. Many devotees enter a state of trance and pierce their cheeks, tongue face or other body parts with sharp objects. At Palani, a town around 100km from [Madurai](https://www.travellerspoint.com/guide/Madurai/), the Thaipsum festivities are on a grand scale and extensive continuing for a period of 10 days.The devotes with piercing all over the body carry a “Kavadi” on their shoulder and carry in a trance like manner to the temple. Kavadi is a cage like structure weighing upto 15 kilograms and is decorated with peacock feathers and aluminum plates which show images of Hindu deities. It requires great endurance to walk and dance with the Kavadis. The Kavadi procession is joined by young children carrying pots of milk.
- **Republic Day** - Republic Day is a national holiday in India every January 26 to commemorate the adoption of the Constitution in 1950 and the declaration of independence in 1930. The capital of New Delhi is the focus of the celebrations, including a flag raising ceremony, wreath laying, 21-gun salute, Presidential speech, and presentation of awards for selflessness and bravery. A massive military parade includes elephants ridden by children who have received national accolades.
- **Gandhi Jayanti** - Gandhi Jayanti is a national public holiday commemorating the birth of the peaceful activist, Mohandas Gandhi on October 2, 1869. The celebration coincides with the United Nations’ International Day of Non-Violence. In India, Gandhi is remembered through statues, flower and candle offerings, prayers and singing the devotional hymn Raghupati Raghava Raja Ram. The Indian government issues special mint rupees and postage stamps bearing his picture.
- **Onam** - The traditional 10-day Onam harvest festival takes place in Kerala during August or September and marks the return of the mythical King Mahabali. The Hindu celebration welcomes the monarch by arranging flowers outside their houses, wearing new clothes, feasting, dancing, and racing in snake boats.
- **Ganesh Chaturthi** - The ten-day September festival of Ganesh Chaturthi celebrates the birthday of the elephant-headed Hindu god Ganesh with culture, concerts and feasts. The biggest events take place in Maharashtra where people worship an idol for ten days before taking it to the river or sea and drowning it.
- **Navarathri, Dussehra Festival** - This theatrical Hindu festival takes place over ten days in October. The first nine feature dancing to honor the Mother Goddess. The tenth day commemorates Lord Rama’s defeat of demon king Ravana and goddess Durga’s triumph over Mahishasura, the buffalo demon. The event is called Durga Puja in east India where the faithful create huge statues to immerse in the Ganges River.
- **Diwali** - Diwali is the five-day festival of lights held in India in late October or early November each year. The widely celebrated Hindu event marks Lord Rama’s victory over the demon Ravan. Homes and streets are decorated with lights, candles and small clay lamps, and new clothes are worn and sweets are exchanged.

## Weather

India is a huge country and although there are similarities in the weather, of course there are differences regarding temperatures and rainfall between the south and north and between the lower parts and the higher Himalaya.  
In general, from June to October the country is influenced by wet monsoon from the southwest. On some mountain ranges rainfall can be very heavy and some areas have over 10,000 mm a year, the wettest places on earth are located here, like [Cherrapunji](https://www.travellerspoint.com/guide/Cherrapunji/), in [Meghalaya](https://www.travellerspoint.com/guide/Meghalaya/), the northeastern most part of the country.  
The coolest, driest time over most of the country is from December to February, when light northerly winds bring clear skies and little rain. From March to May, India becomes hotter and hotter and the drought continues. The rains only come when the wind turns again to the southwest. On average, the arrival of the rains comes to the south of India during late May or early June and reaches the north about six weeks later.

The southern parts of India, like [Kerala](https://www.travellerspoint.com/guide/Kerala/), are more tropical with hot and humid conditions year round. Temperatures are around or above 20 °C at night, while days are generally above 30 °C. Temperatures can reach well over 40 °C though. Coastal areas are wetter compared to the inland areas. Also, they have less extreme temperatures, especially along the west coast. [Chennai](https://www.travellerspoint.com/guide/Chennai/) (Madras) at the east coast can have temperatures well over 40 °C as well though.

The north is extremely hot from March to May, with temperatures sometimes exceeding 50 °C in [Rajasthan](https://www.travellerspoint.com/guide/Rajasthan/), and averages are well into the 40's. Generally, from west to east temperatures are less extreme and there is more rainfall. Calcutta ([Kolkata](https://www.travellerspoint.com/guide/Kolkata/)) for example is much wetter than Delhi and this applies to the mountains in the west and east as well. Nights in the northwest during winter (December to February) can drop to only a few degrees above zero.

In the northernmost Himalayan mountain ranges, summers are very pleasant, with less rain and more sun, but winters can be bitterly cold, with frost and snow. Temperatures can drop well below \-10 °C at night and average a pleasant 30 °C in Srinagar for example. The highest peaks are always cold, but trekking in [Ladakh](https://www.travellerspoint.com/guide/Ladakh/) is very comfortable during June to September.
